coverage_gaps: Need live public-company universe expansion across U.S., Canada, Europe, Japan, Taiwan, Korea, and Singapore for small/mid-cap suppliers.
Need market-pricing check: analyst coverage count, market cap, liquidity, recent share-price move, valuation, and short interest for each candidate.
Need primary-source verification from filings, investor decks, earnings calls, customer announcements, capex plans, and segment revenue disclosure.
Need to separate true bottlenecks from cyclical volume beneficiaries, especially in optical modules, OSATs, software, and industrial electrical suppliers.
Need customer/supplier dependency mapping: which small suppliers are qualified by TSMC, memory vendors, hyperscalers, optical module makers, or major data-center contractors.
Need falsification triggers for each node: capacity additions, dual-sourcing, price declines, customer design-outs, order cancellations, margin compression, or regulatory delays.

memory_update.text: Technology theme should be decomposed through AI/cloud demand into physical infrastructure, semiconductor capacity, software control planes, and energy/grid constraints rather than centered on a single mega-cap ticker.
HBM and advanced packaging overflow is a priority underfollowed lane; search beyond memory producers into OSAT, backend test, fan-out packaging, substrates, consumables, and equipment.

Optical interconnect toolchains are a priority lane: lasers, silicon photonics, compound-semiconductor substrates, epitaxy capacity, and MOCVD tools may be less obvious than switch vendors or module assemblers.

High-purity semiconductor materials such as quartz, crucibles, wafers, ceramics, filters, and specialty consumables may represent hidden dependencies but require careful public-asset mapping because direct assets can be private or buried in subsidiaries.

Data-center power and thermal infrastructure should be screened one layer below obvious leaders into switchgear components, busway, UPS, transformers, liquid-cooling parts, heat exchangers, pumps, sensors, and engineering services.
Cloud security and automation software is a non-semiconductor second-order lane tied to AI workload sprawl, machine identities, API growth, observability, data governance, and compliance.

Later layers must collect primary-source evidence and market-pricing data before ranking companies: filings, earnings calls, segment revenue, customer qualification, capex, backlog, analyst coverage, valuation, and liquidity.

summary: Layer 1A decomposes the broad Technology theme into six researchable supply-chain nodes where obvious AI/cloud demand may create second-order beneficiaries. The strongest decomposition lanes are: advanced memory and packaging overflow, optical interconnect toolchains, semiconductor substrate/material chokepoints, data-center power/thermal infrastructure, cloud/security automation software tied to AI workload sprawl, and grid/nuclear fuel infrastructure. This is not a stock recommendation layer; it is a theme funnel map for later evidence collection, public-company screening, pricing checks, and falsification.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: HBM producers and advanced packaging leaders may be well priced, but conventional DRAM/NAND backend, HBM-adjacent test, fan-out panel-level packaging, and overflow OSAT capacity could become second-order beneficiaries with less obvious market labels.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prefer USD 300M-10B market cap OSAT/test/material names; include USD 10B-30B only if AI packaging exposure is unusually pure. Reject names whose thesis depends only on broad memory-cycle beta without evidence of advanced-package or HBM-adjacent capacity.
supply_chain_nodes.node: HBM, advanced packaging, OSAT, and backend memory-test overflow
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Screen Taiwan, Korea, Japan, Singapore, and U.S.-listed OSATs, test handlers, substrate suppliers, bonding/tool vendors, thermal interface material suppliers, and advanced-packaging consumables. Use Powertech-like examples as a pattern, not as the only candidate.

supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: AI accelerators depend on memory bandwidth and advanced packaging; if HBM and packaging capacity remain tight, overflow work can move to third-party packaging and testing providers instead of only benefiting obvious memory producers.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The market may first price switch vendors and optical module assemblers, while the harder-to-map bottleneck could sit in qualified epitaxy capacity, indium phosphide or gallium arsenide substrates, laser production tools, silicon-photonics foundry capacity, or test equipment.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Target USD 1B-15B equipment/material/component companies; avoid assuming all optics exposure is scarce because module assembly can be competitive. Later layers must test whether capacity is genuinely constrained versus merely benefiting from volume growth.

Include Aixtron-like toolmakers as an indirect bottleneck lane.

supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: AI cluster scaling increases east-west data movement, raising demand for high-speed optical links, transceivers, lasers, silicon photonics, and potentially co-packaged optics. Toolmakers and compound-semiconductor inputs can benefit from many downstream winners expanding capacity.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The most obscure bottlenecks may not be chips or equipment but upstream materials such as high-purity quartz, quartz crucibles, wafer inputs, specialty gases, filters, ceramics, and contamination-control components.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Use USD 300M-10B as the preferred range, but allow larger diversified chemical/materials firms only if segment disclosure or customer evidence shows semiconductor-grade exposure. Treat micro-caps as speculative exceptions unless they disclose qualification status and customer concentration.

supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Start from known choke examples such as Spruce Pine high-purity quartz, then map to public suppliers in quartz products, crucibles, wafers, specialty materials, ceramics, filtration, and process consumables. Many direct assets may be private or embedded inside larger conglomerates, so public-market mapping should include suppliers to the suppliers.

supply_chain_nodes.underfollowed_angle: The assets may be obscure because the critical material operation is private, buried in a subsidiary, or too small inside a diversified company. This makes evidence collection harder but also improves the chance of finding hidden dependencies.
supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: Semiconductor manufacturing depends on highly qualified upstream materials. Some inputs are invisible to most AI and semiconductor screens but can have limited sources, long qualification cycles, and high switching costs.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: Obvious winners such as Vertiv and Eaton may already be well followed, but second-order beneficiaries could include smaller suppliers of switchgear components, thermal management parts, electrical enclosures, busbars, heat exchangers, pumps, sensors, monitoring software, and engineering services.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prioritize USD 500M-10B electrical/thermal specialists with rising data-center backlog, margin expansion, or capacity additions. Avoid firms where data-center revenue is too small or indistinguishable from normal construction cyclicality.

Prioritize recurring revenue, retention, and mission-critical workflow integration over generic AI branding.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Run a two-lane funnel. Use mega-cap reference leaders only to validate demand direction and capex signal: NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, ASML, Arista, Vertiv, Eaton, Constellation, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta. The alpha-hunting lane should deliberately search one to three steps upstream or adjacent: sub-$50B HBM/advanced-packaging suppliers, OSATs, test handlers, quartz/crucible/wafer inputs, epitaxy tools, compound-semiconductor substrates, optical module contract manufacturers, power-electrical component vendors, data-center engineering services, cybersecurity automation vendors, and niche software suppliers with low analyst coverage. Later layers should compare valuation/pricing to evidence strength and reject names where the market has already fully identified the bottleneck.
supply_side_constraints: Advanced-node foundry and advanced packaging capacity concentration
HBM structural undersupply and crowding-out of conventional DRAM/NAND backend capacity
Qualification cycles for semiconductor materials, substrates, optics, lasers, and equipment
Limited supplier bases in ultra-pure semiconductor materials such as high-purity quartz and quartz crucibles
Long lead times for data-center electrical equipment, transformers, switchgear, and power/cooling systems
Regulatory and licensing constraints in nuclear fuel, grid interconnection, and power generation
